extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy of science; general educated readers interested in scientific method and epistemology
extracted.subtask_description: A textbook chapter examining the nature and meaning of scientific law, the relation between perception and reason, the limits of scientific inference (especially about the supersensuous), and the distinction between description (science) and prescriptive or theological claims. It develops criteria for what counts as scientific law, cause, and explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature of scientific law
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific law is a brief description in mental shorthand of as wide a range as possible of the sequences of our sense-impressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scientific law is descriptive, not prescriptive: it does not imply an intelligent lawgiver, command, or duty. It summarizes repeated sequences of perceptions into concise formulae rather than demonstrating any inherent necessity in those sequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two meanings of natural law
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two distinct meanings to natural law: the mere routine of perception (nomic) and the scientific law (the concise descriptive formulae of nature).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'reason' we attribute to natural law is only obvious for the scientific-law sense and is placed there by the human mind; we cannot legitimately project that reason beyond sense-impressions into the supersensuous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perceptive faculty as source of perceptual routine
rubrics_metrics.description: The routine of our perceptions may be due to the structure and selectivity of the perceptive faculty itself (the mind as a 'sorting-machine').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because perceptive systems are selective (examples: differences between man and dog; evolutionary shaping of perception), the regularities science describes may originate in our perceptive machinery rather than in 'dead matter' outside perception. This suggests analyzing perception itself is central to understanding natural law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordination of perceptive and reflective faculties
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific success depends on the co-development and coordination of the perceptive (selecting) and reflective (analyzing) faculties; the reflective faculty resumes perceptions into brief formulae or laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Within limits the intensity of perception is proportional to reasoning; defects in coordination (e.g., idiocy, insanity) impair analysis. The reflective faculty can only analyze those perceptions that the perceptive faculty selects and that are amenable to analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity of scientific law partly conditioned by sensory channels
rubrics_metrics.description: The apparent simplicity of scientific law may be partly conditioned by the simplicity of the modes in which sense-impressions are received (few and comparatively simple sensory channels).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because impressions arrive through limited channels (vision, hearing, touch), the laws that summarize them tend toward simpler, more general descriptions; this is a factor to consider when evaluating why laws are concise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Science describes past experience; prediction is probabilistic belief
rubrics_metrics.description: Science for the past is a description; for the future it is a belief expressed by the concept of probability. Science cannot demonstrate any inherent necessity in a sequence of sense-impressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: We may assert overwhelming probability that past-regularities will continue, but science cannot prove absolute necessity; treat explanations as summaries of experience and predictions as probabilistic judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanics as descriptive science (avoid 'dead mechanism' misinterpretation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mechanics is the science of motion defined as the complete description in the simplest possible manner of such motions as occur in nature; it is descriptive, not a claim of inherent necessity or a 'dead' agent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not contrast the 'mechanical' with the 'intellectual' when mechanics is properly understood; laws of motion, like biological laws, are intellectual products summarizing experience, differing mainly in generality and simplicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Force as cause is ambiguous and not a scientific explanatory ultimate
rubrics_metrics.description: Treating force as a cause that necessitates a routine of perceptions leads to unintelligibility: force may be unknowable (if beyond perception) or unknown (if due to perceptive structure).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because 'cause' and 'force' carry multiple ideas, avoid invoking force as an ultimate explanatory agent without clarifying whether one means an unknowable metaphysical source or an empirical factor within perception; scientific conceptions of cause must be careful and precise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Science must remain agnostic about the supersensuous
rubrics_metrics.description: Beyond the barrier of sense-impression science can logically infer only chaos; we have no ground for projecting human conceptions of order, reason, or consciousness into the supersensuous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Natural theology and metaphysics that assert reason can access the supersensuous are pseudo-scientific; science should not assert claims about what lies beyond sense-impressions and must remonstrate where belief replaces knowledge as a basis of conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer honest admission of ignorance over speculative hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Wherescience has not yet described phenomena in concise formulae, the correct course is honest confession of ignorance rather than assuming or hypothecating supersensuous causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid replacing ignorance by hypothesis prematurely; historical examples (origin of species, weather) show that phenomena within sense-impressions often yield to scientific analysis over time. Hypotheses about the supersensuous should be withheld until known causes are shown insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminology must be used with precise meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Words like 'explain' and 'explanation' should be used to mean descriptive 'how' (describing in brief formula) rather than determinative 'why'; lack of precision in terms leads to confusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Insist on concise meanings and clearly defined limits when employing terms in scientific discourse to avoid muddled speculation and category errors between belief and knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific law is an intellectual product of man
rubrics_metrics.description: The nomic routine of perception is an unconscious product of the perceptive machinery, while natural law in the scientific sense is the conscious product of the reflective faculty — thus natural law appears an intellectual product of man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that the attribution of reason to natural law is a placement by the human mind; scientists should be aware that their laws summarize human perceptions and rationalizations rather than necessarily mirroring an independent rationality in 'things-in-themselves.'
